claim: The magnitude of the autocorrelation of intrinsic neural signals in a brain area reflects how long neural information is stored in that local region.
source: How long neural information is stored in a local brain area reflects functions of that region and is often estimated by the magnitude of the autocorrelation of intrinsic neural signals in the area.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on intrinsic neural timescales and temporal receptive windows.

claim: High-functioning adults with autism have shorter neural timescales in the sensory/visual cortices.
source: By analysing resting-state fMRI data, we identified shorter neural timescales in the sensory/visual cortices and a longer timescale in the right caudate in autism.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fMRI data analysis comparing ASD and TD groups.

claim: High-functioning adults with autism have a longer neural timescale in the right caudate.
source: By analysing resting-state fMRI data, we identified shorter neural timescales in the sensory/visual cortices and a longer timescale in the right caudate in autism.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fMRI data analysis comparing ASD and TD groups.

claim: Shorter intrinsic timescales in the sensory/visual areas are correlated with the severity of autism.
source: The shorter intrinsic timescales in the sensory/visual areas were correlated with the severity of autism, whereas the longer timescale in the caudate was associated with cognitive rigidity.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between neural timescales and ADOS scores.

claim: Longer intrinsic timescale in the caudate is associated with cognitive rigidity in autism.
source: The shorter intrinsic timescales in the sensory/visual areas were correlated with the severity of autism, whereas the longer timescale in the caudate was associated with cognitive rigidity.
evidence: This is supported by association analysis between neural timescales and RRB symptoms.

claim: The intrinsic timescale is correlated with local grey matter volume.
source: Moreover, the intrinsic timescale was correlated with local grey matter volume.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between timescales and GMV measurements.

claim: Functional and structural atypicality in local brain areas is linked to higher-order cognitive symptoms in autism.
source: This study shows that functional and structural atypicality in local brain areas is linked to higher-order cognitive symptoms in autism.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined findings of timescale-GMV correlations and timescale-symptom associations.

claim: Neural timescales show a rostrocaudal gradient in the brain.
source: Computational studies propose that such neural timescales should show a rostrocaudal gradient in the brains (Kiebel et al., 2008) and that densely interconnected central regions, such as prefrontal and parietal areas, should have slower timescales compared to peripheral sensory areas (Chaudhuri et al., 2015; Gollo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to computational studies.

claim: Densely interconnected central regions such as prefrontal and parietal areas have slower timescales compared to peripheral sensory areas.
source: Computational studies propose that such neural timescales should show a rostrocaudal gradient in the brains (Kiebel et al., 2008) and that densely interconnected central regions, such as prefrontal and parietal areas, should have slower timescales compared to peripheral sensory areas (Chaudhuri et al., 2015; Gollo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to computational studies.

claim: Neural timescales tend to be longer in frontal and parietal areas compared to sensory-related regions in humans and macaques.
source: Human neuroimaging and macaque electrophysiology studies show that neural timescales tend to be longer in frontal and parietal areas compared to sensory-related regions (Honey et al., 2012; Stephens et al., 2013; Murray et al., 2014; Ogawa and Komatsu, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical neuroimaging and electrophysiology studies.

claim: Prolonged neural timescale enables higher-order brain cortices to integrate diverse information for robust sensory perception.
source: and suggested that such a prolonged neural timescale enables these higher-order brain cortices to integrate diverse information for robust sensory perception (Hasson et al., 2008; Lerner et al., 2011; Stephens et al., 2013; Yeshurun et al., 2017; Ogawa and Komatsu, 2010; Gauthier et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Prolonged neural timescale enables stable memory processing.
source: stable memory processing (Hasson et al., 2015; Murray et al., 2014; Bernacchia et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Prolonged neural timescale enables accurate decision making.
source: and accurate decision making (Cavanagh et al., 2016; Runyan et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The hierarchy of the intrinsic timescale is closely related to functional interactions between lower and higher brain regions.
source: A recent brain stimulation study directly demonstrates that such a hierarchy of the intrinsic timescale is closely related to functional interactions between lower and higher brain regions (Cocchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a brain stimulation study.

claim: The heterogeneity of the neural timescale is considered to be a basis of the functional hierarchy in the brain.
source: The heterogeneity of the neural timescale is considered to be a basis of the functional hierarchy in the brain (Chen et al., 2015; Hasson et al., 2015; Himberger et al., 2018; Chaudhuri et al., 2015; Gollo et al., 2015; Cocchi et al., 2016; Kukushkin and Carew, 2017; Friston and Kiebel, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Autism is associated with impairments of the global integration of diverse information and over-enhancement of individual inputs according to weak coherence theory.
source: weak coherence theory suggests that autism spectral disorder (ASD) is associated with impairments of the global integration of diverse information and over-enhancement of individual inputs (Happé and Frith, 2006; Booth and Happé, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to weak coherence theory studies.

claim: A Bayesian view attributes autism to overweighing of local sensory information.
source: a recent Bayesian view also attributes autism to overweighing of local sensory information (Palmer et al., 2017; Lawson et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bayesian theory studies.

claim: No study has investigated intrinsic timescales of neural signals in autism prior to this work.
source: Despite such theoretical implications, no study has investigated intrinsic timescales of neural signals in autism.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature at the time of the study.

claim: The fMRI-based intrinsic timescale scores were highly correlated with those calculated from simultaneously recorded EEG data in the gamma band (adjusted R² = 0.71).
source: fMRI-based intrinsic timescale scores were highly correlated with those calculated from simultaneously recorded EEG data (gamma band, adjusted R2 = 0.71; panel b; see Figure 1—figure supplement 2 for other EEG bands).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between fMRI and EEG data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The fMRI-based timescales were different from those based on the EEG data by two orders of magnitude.
source: The fMRI-based timescales were different from those based on the EEG data by two orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is observed from the comparison of fMRI and EEG timescale measurements.

claim: When EEG signals were convolved with the hemodynamic response function (HRF), the intrinsic timescales based on EEG data showed the same magnitude as those based on fMRI data.
source: When we convolved the EEG signals with the hemodynamic response function (HRF), the intrinsic timescales based on EEG data showed the same magnitude as those based on fMRI data (panel c).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Both ASD and TD groups showed a similar whole-brain pattern of intrinsic neural timescales with longer timescales in frontal and parietal cortices and shorter timescales in sensorimotor, visual, and auditory areas.
source: Both ASD and TD groups showed a similar whole-brain pattern of intrinsic neural timescales: longer timescales in frontal and parietal cortices and shorter timescales in sensorimotor, visual, and auditory areas (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The observed whole-brain pattern of intrinsic neural timescales is consistent with previous reports about hierarchical topography of timescales in mice, monkeys, and humans.
source: This observation is consistent with previous reports about a hierarchal topography of timescales of local neural activity in brains of mice (Runyan et al., 2017), monkeys (Chaudhuri et al., 2015; Murray et al., 2014; Ogawa and Komatsu, 2010), and humans (Hasson et al., 2008; Honey et al., 2012; Lerner et al., 2011; Stephens et al., 2013; Yeshurun et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies in multiple species.

claim: Individuals with ASD had significantly shorter intrinsic timescales in bilateral postcentral gyri, right inferior parietal lobule (IPL), right middle insula, bilateral middle temporal gyri (MTG), and right inferior occipital gyrus (IOG) compared to TD individuals.
source: Individuals with ASD had a significantly shorter intrinsic timescale than TD individuals in bilateral postcentral gyri, right inferior parietal lobule (IPL), right middle insula, bilateral middle temporal gyri (MTG), and right inferior occipital gyrus (IOG) (Figure 2b and d)
evidence: This is supported by whole-brain analysis with FDR correction shown in Figure 2b and d.

claim: The intrinsic timescale in the right caudate was significantly larger in the ASD group compared to the TD group.
source: whereas the intrinsic timescale in the right caudate was significantly larger in the ASD group (Figure 2c and e).
evidence: This is supported by whole-brain analysis shown in Figure 2c and e.

claim: The bilateral postcentral gyri and right IOG showed negative correlations between the intrinsic timescale and overall severity of autism (rho ≤ –0.49, Puncorrected <0.01, PFDR <0.05).
source: Of the seven brain regions of interest (ROIs) whose intrinsic timescales were shorter in the ASD group (Figure 2b and d, Table 2), the bilateral postcentral gyri and right IOG showed negative correlations between the intrinsic timescale and overall severity of autism (rho ≤ –0.49, Puncorrected <0.01, PFDR <0.05; Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The right caudate did not show an association with the overall ADOS score (rho = 0.19, p=0.34).
source: The right caudate, a single ROI whose intrinsic timescale was significantly longer in the ASD group (Figure 2e), did not show such an association with the overall ADOS score (rho = 0.19, p=0.34).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: The intrinsic timescale in the right caudate was longer in individuals with more severe repetitive, restricted behaviours (F3,21 = 9.9, p<0.001; Spearman's rho = 0.57, p=0.002).
source: However, its intrinsic timescale was longer in individuals with more severe repetitive, restricted behaviours (RRB), as measured by ADOS RRB scores (F3,21 = 9.9, p<0.001, main effect of ADOS RRB in a one-way ANOVA; Spearman's rho = 0.57, p=0.002; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by ANOVA and correlation analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The brain-symptom associations were preserved when analyzed in two independent fMRI datasets (ETH Zürich and Indiana University datasets) that were not used in the ROI search.
source: These brain-symptom associations were preserved even when we conducted this association analysis in a more statistically rigorous manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). That is, we applied the same ROI sets to two independent fMRI datasets (ETH Zürich and Indiana University datasets; Supplementary Table 1 in Supplementary file 1) that were not used in the ROI search, and found negative correlations between the intrinsic timescales and the ADOS total scores in the bilateral postcentral gyri and right IOG (rho ≤ –0.60) and a significant association between the intrinsic timescale and the ADOS RRB scores in the right caudate (F ≥ 6.0, p≤0.03 in one-way ANOVAs).
evidence: This is supported by replication analysis in independent datasets shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In adolescence, the intrinsic neural timescale in bilateral postcentral gyri and right IOG was consistently shorter in individuals with ASD compared to TD individuals (F1,31 > 9.0, Puncorrected <0.005, PFDR <0.05).
source: In adolescence, we found that the intrinsic neural timescale in bilateral postcentral gyri and right IOG was consistently shorter in individuals with ASD compared to TD individuals (F1,31 > 9.0, Puncorrected <0.005, PFDR <0.05, main effect of diagnosis in repeated-measures two-way ANOVAs with a diagnosis [ASD/TD] × scan order [1 st/2nd] structure; Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The decreases in the intrinsic timescale in bilateral postcentral gyri and right IOG during adolescence were predictive of the increases in the overall severity of autism (rho ≤ –0.68, Puncorrected <0.003, PFDR <0.05).
source: In addition, the decreases in the intrinsic timescale in these areas during this period were predictive of the increases in the overall severity of autism (rho ≤ –0.68, Puncorrected <0.003, PFDR <0.05; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal correlation analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The intrinsic timescale in the right caudate was consistently longer in the ASD group during adolescence (F1,31 = 18.2, Puncorrected <0.001).
source: In contrast, the intrinsic timescale in the right caudate was consistently longer in the group with ASD during adolescence (F1,31 = 18.2, Puncorrected <0.001, main effect of diagnosis in a repeated-measures two-way ANOVA; Figure 4c)
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The increase in the intrinsic timescale in the right caudate was associated with progression of RRB symptoms (F2,8 = 10.3, p=0.006).
source: and the increase in the intrinsic timescale in this region was associated with progression of RRB symptoms (F2,8 = 10.3, p=0.006, main effect of ADOS RRB changes in a one-way ANOVA; Figure 4d).
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Autistic atypicality of temporal neural processing in local brain areas may already occur before adolescence.
source: These longitudinal observations are consistent with the cross-sectional findings (Figures 2 and 3) and suggest that autistic atypicality of temporal neural processing in local brain areas may already occur before adolescence.
evidence: This is inferred from the longitudinal findings showing consistent differences during adolescence.

claim: An increase in neuronal density, which is measured by GMV, would enhance recurrent neural network activity, and then enlarge the autocorrelation strength in the neural signals.
source: We focused on GMV because theoretically, an increase in neuronal density, which is measured by GMV (Kanai and Rees, 2011), would enhance recurrent neural network activity, and then enlarge the autocorrelation strength in the neural signals.
evidence: This is a theoretical assumption supported by citation and logical inference.

claim: At a group level, intrinsic timescale and GMV were positively correlated with each other across 360 brain areas (TD: r = 0.40, ASD: r = 0.38, p<10–5).
source: This theoretical assumption was validated by comparisons between intrinsic timescales and GMV across 360 brain areas (Glasser et al., 2016): at a group level, these functional and anatomical properties were positively correlated with each other (TD: r = 0.40, ASD: r = 0.38, p<10–5; Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The significant correlations between intrinsic timescale and GMV were robustly observed at a single-participant level (TD: r ≥ 0.29, ASD: r ≥ 0.28, p<10–5).
source: Furthermore, the significant correlations were robustly observed at a single-participant level as well (TD: r ≥ 0.29, ASD: r ≥ 0.28, p<10–5; Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by single-participant correlation analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The association between intrinsic timescale and GMV was seen in the four brain regions whose atypical intrinsic neural timescale was associated with symptoms of autism (r > 0.52, p≤0.005).
source: This association was also seen in the four brain regions whose atypical intrinsic neural timescale was associated with symptoms of autism (r > 0.52, p≤0.005; Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The GMVs of the three brain regions showing atypical reduction in the intrinsic timescale in autism were significantly smaller in the ASD than the TD group.
source: Given these findings together with atypical GMVs in the four brain regions in individuals with ASD (t49 >3.0, Puncorrected ≤0.004 in two-sample t-tests, PFDR <0.05; Figure 5d)
evidence: This is supported by group comparison analysis shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The GMV of the right caudate, which had an atypically longer intrinsic timescale in autism, was larger in the ASD group.
source: Given these findings together with atypical GMVs in the four brain regions in individuals with ASD (t49 >3.0, Puncorrected ≤0.004 in two-sample t-tests, PFDR <0.05; Figure 5d)
evidence: This is supported by group comparison analysis shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Intrinsic neural timescale is a mediator linking atypical GMV and ASD symptoms.
source: Given these findings together with atypical GMVs in the four brain regions in individuals with ASD (t49 >3.0, Puncorrected ≤0.004 in two-sample t-tests, PFDR <0.05; Figure 5d), we can infer that intrinsic neural timescale is a mediator linking atypical GMV and ASD symptoms. This inference was, in fact, consistent with results of mediation analyses (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is supported by mediation analysis shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The main findings were replicated in two independent MRI datasets obtained from adults with ASD, collected in ETH Zürich and Indiana University.
source: We replicated our findings in the two independent MRI datasets obtained from adults with ASD, which were collected in ETH Zürich and Indiana University (Supplementary Table 1 in Supplementary file 1) (Di Martino et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by replication analyses in independent datasets.

claim: In both ETH Zürich and Indiana University datasets, ASD group yielded atypically shorter intrinsic timescales in the bilateral postcentral gyri and right IOG (t ≥ 4.0, PFDR <0.05).
source: In both datasets, ASD group yielded atypically shorter intrinsic timescales in the bilateral postcentral gyri and right IOG (t ≥ 4.0, PFDR <0.05; Figure 5—figure supplements 1a and 2a)
evidence: This is supported by replication analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1a and 2a.

claim: In both ETH Zürich and Indiana University datasets, ASD group showed a longer intrinsic timescale in the right caudate (t = 3.9, PFDR <0.05).
source: and a longer intrinsic timescale in the right caudate (t = 3.9, PFDR <0.05; Figure 5—figure supplements 1b and 2b).
evidence: This is supported by replication analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1b and 2b.

claim: In both replication datasets, the shorter intrinsic timescale in the bilateral postcentral gyri and right IOG was correlated with the overall severity of ASD (rho ≤ –0.51).
source: The shorter intrinsic timescale in the bilateral postcentral gyri and right IOG was correlated with the overall severity of ASD (rho ≤ –0.51; Figure 5—figure supplements 1c and 2c)
evidence: This is supported by replication analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1c and 2c.

claim: In both replication datasets, the longer intrinsic timescale in the caudate was associated with RRB symptoms (p<0.028 in one-way ANOVAs; Spearman's rho ≥0.74).
source: whereas the longer intrinsic timescale in the caudate was associated with RRB symptoms (p<0.028 in one-way ANOVAs; Spearman's rho ≥0.74; Figure 5—figure supplements 1d and 2d).
evidence: This is supported by replication analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1d and 2d.

claim: The correlations between the intrinsic timescale and GMV were replicated in both independent datasets (r ≥ 0.49).
source: Moreover, the correlations between the intrinsic timescale and GMV were also replicated (r ≥ 0.49; Figure 5—figure supplements 1e and 2e).
evidence: This is supported by replication analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1e and 2e.

claim: The atypically short intrinsic timescale in the primary sensory/visual cortices observed in the ASD group might potentially be one of neural bases of perceptual hyper-sensitivity often seen in autism.
source: Given this, we speculate that the atypically short intrinsic timescale in the primary sensory/visual cortices observed in the ASD group (Figures 2b and 4a) might potentially be one of neural bases of perceptual hyper-sensitivity often seen in autism (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data and theoretical considerations.

claim: Large GMVs indicate a high density of neurons in local brain regions.
source: Large GMVs are considered to indicate a high density of neurons in local brain regions (Kanai and Rees, 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: High neuronal density is thought to be accompanied with more synapses.
source: which is thought to be accompanied with more synapses (Cullen et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: High neuronal density is thought to be accompanied with greater synaptic weights.
source: and greater synaptic weights (Perin et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: High neuronal and synaptic density should increase reciprocal connections within brain areas and enhance local clustering.
source: Moreover, computational studies suggest that such a high neuronal and synaptic density should increase reciprocal connections within the areas and enhance local clustering (Perin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to computational studies.

claim: Spontaneous neural activity largely depends on recurrent neural networks.
source: Given that spontaneous neural activity largely depends on such recurrent neural networks (Ikegaya et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Resting-state neural activities of brain regions with large GMVs would show more repetition patterns and larger autocorrelations.
source: resting-state neural activities of brain regions with large GMVs would show more repetition patterns and larger autocorrelations.
evidence: This is inferred from the theoretical considerations about neuronal density, synaptic connections, and recurrent networks.

claim: fMRI studies found atypically large signal variability in the prefrontal region in individuals with ASD.
source: For example, fMRI studies that investigated intra-participant variability of brain signals across time found atypically large signal variability in the prefrontal region (Dinstein et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous fMRI studies.

claim: fMRI studies found atypically large signal variability in the somato-sensory area in individuals with ASD.
source: somato-sensory area (Haigh et al., 2015; Dinstein et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous fMRI studies.

claim: fMRI studies found atypically large signal variability in the auditory area in individuals with ASD.
source: auditory area (Haigh et al., 2015; Dinstein et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous fMRI studies.

claim: fMRI studies found atypically large signal variability in the primary visual cortex in individuals with ASD.
source: and primary visual cortex (Dinstein et al., 2012; Dinstein et al., 2010; Milne, 2011) in individuals with ASD.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous fMRI studies.

claim: One study found that the severity of ASD was significantly correlated with atypical signal variability in the sensory/visual areas.
source: In particular, one study found that the severity of ASD was significantly correlated with such atypical signal variability in the sensory/visual areas (Dinstein et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The neuroanatomical association between the caudate and the RRB symptoms was reported in previous structural MRI studies.
source: In fact, the neuroanatomical association between the subcortical region and the RRB symptoms was reported in previous structural MRI studies (Langen et al., 2014; Langen et al., 2009; Langen et al., 2007; Hollander et al., 2005; Schuetze et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural MRI studies.

claim: No prior research has been conducted on intrinsic neural timescales or signal variability of the caudate in autism.
source: However, to the best of our knowledge, no prior research has been conducted on intrinsic neural timescales or signal variability of the caudate in autism.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: The intrinsic timescale and TRW is not an artefact of neuroimaging signals but closely associated with an ability of local brain areas to pool, normalise, and complete information.
source: A recent review has suggested that the intrinsic timescale and TRW is not an artefact of neuroimaging signals but closely associated with an ability of local brain areas to pool, normalise, and complete information (Himberger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent review.

claim: For sensory information processing, a longer neural timescale is considered to make brain responses more robust against fluctuations in sensory inputs and enable steady and consistent perception.
source: In particular, for sensory information processing, a longer neural timescale is considered to make brain responses more robust against fluctuations in sensory inputs and enable steady and consistent perception (Himberger et al., 2018; Honey et al., 2012; Murray et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The study analyzed resting-state fMRI data from 25 high-functioning adults with ASD and 26 age-/sex-/IQ-matched typically developing individuals.
source: Based on this formulation, we compared the intrinsic neural timescale between 25 high-functioning adults with ASD and 26 age-/sex-/IQ-matched typically developing (TD) individuals (Table 1) (Di Martino et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the study design and sample.

claim: The study used a longitudinal fMRI dataset with two MRI scans for each participant, with an interval of 2.8 ± 0.4 years for ASD children and 3.0 ± 0.4 years for TD children.
source: To this end, we analysed a longitudinal fMRI dataset recorded from adolescent children (two MRI scans for each participant, interval of the two scans = 2.8 ± 0.4 years for ASD children, 3.0 ± 0.4 years for TD children; Supplementary Table 2 in Supplementary file 1) (Di Martino et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the longitudinal study design.

claim: The preprocessing succeeded in significantly reducing the fMRI-induced noise in the EEG data.
source: Both panels suggest that the preprocessing succeeded in significantly reducing the fMRI-induced noise in the EEG data.
evidence: This is supported by power spectra analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Relatively large correlations between fMRI-based and EEG-based intrinsic timescales were found in the alpha and beta bands.
source: As shown in Figure 1c, the fMRI-based intrinsic timescale was strongly correlated with those based on the gamma band of EEG signals. We also examined such correlations for different EEG bands, and relatively large correlations in the alpha and beta bands.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A significant correlation between fMRI-based and EEG-based intrinsic timescales was seen without band filtering (R²*=0.40).
source: A significant correlation was also seen without band filtering (R2*=0.40).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: When the EEG signals were convolved with the HRF, the intrinsic timescales based on the HRF-convolved EEG signals became closer to those based on fMRI signals (adjusted R² = 0.61).
source: In addition, when the EEG signals were convolved with the hemodynamic response function (HRF), the intrinsic timescales based on the HRF-convolved EEG signals became closer to those based on fMRI signals (adjusted R2 = 0.61; Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1c.

claim: An EEG signal is likely to peak ~100 ms after a stimulus onset.
source: Moreover, such a difference would be reasonable because an EEG signal is likely to peak ~100 ms after a stimulus onset
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about EEG signal timing.

claim: An fMRI signal tends to take 5 ~ 10 s to peak.
source: and an fMRI signal — a product of neurovascular coupling (Hillman, 2014; Martindale et al., 2003) — tends to take 5 ~ 10 s to peak (Logothetis et al., 2001; Yeşilyurt et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on hemodynamic response.

claim: The fMRI-based neural timescales represent an aspect of local neuronal activity.
source: These EEG-fMRI comparisons indicate that the fMRI-based neural timescales represent an aspect of local neuronal activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the validation analysis comparing fMRI and EEG timescales.

claim: It is beyond the scope of this study to conclude that the fMRI-based index reflects the same neuronal phenomena as those seen in previous electrophysiology work that calculated neural timescales from spike activity data.
source: However, it is beyond the scope of this study to conclude that such an fMRI-based index reflects the same neuronal phenomena as those seen in previous electrophysiology work that calculated neural timescales from spike activity data (Cavanagh et al., 2016; Murray et al., 2014; Ogawa and Komatsu, 2010; Runyan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study.

claim: Future studies have to directly compare the fMRI-based neural timescales with those based on neuronal spike activities that are collected simultaneously with fMRI data.
source: To clarify this issue, future studies have to directly compare the fMRI-based neural timescales with those based on neuronal spike activities that are collected simultaneously with fMRI data.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: Biological mechanisms underlying the brain-behaviour link between local brain dynamics and behavioural tendencies in autism remain unknown.
source: Our exploratory study identified significant associations between local brain dynamics and behavioural tendencies in autism; however, biological mechanisms underlying this brain-behaviour link remain unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current findings.

claim: Atypical neural timescale may represent atypical functional hierarchy in information processing in brains.
source: Previous work proposed that such an atypical neural timescale may represent atypical functional hierarchy in information processing in brains (Himberger et al., 2018; Chaudhuri et al., 2015; Gjorgjieva et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: It is necessary to directly examine the hypothesis that atypical neural timescale represents atypical functional hierarchy by analysing task-related whole-brain activity in ASD populations.
source: However, it is necessary to directly examine this hypothesis by analysing task-related whole-brain activity in ASD populations.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: Future work needs to investigate mechanisms linking local neural dynamics to atypical large-scale brain dynamics seen in autism.
source: Future work also needs to investigate mechanisms linking these local neural dynamics to atypical large-scale brain dynamics seen in autism (Watanabe and Rees, 2017).
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: The study limited the ASD group to high-functioning right-handed adult males to improve detectability.
source: To improve detectability, we limited the ASD group to high-functioning right-handed adult males.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the study design.

claim: Future studies have to examine the current observations in different subsets of ASD cohorts.
source: Although we confirmed the main findings in an adolescent dataset (Figure 4), future studies have to examine the current observations in different subsets of ASD cohorts.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research to address study limitations.

claim: The study used simultaneous EEG-fMRI data shared in the Open Science Framework for validation.
source: We examined the validity of the current formulation of the intrinsic neural timescales by comparing simultaneously recorded resting-state EEG and fMRI data that were shared in the Open Science Framework (Deligianni et al., 2016; Deligianni et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the data source for validation analysis.

claim: Simultaneous EEG-fMRI data were collected from 17 healthy adults (6 females, 32.84 ± 8.1 years old) at UCL.
source: Simultaneous EEG-fMRI data were collected from 17 healthy adults (6 females, 32.84 ± 8.1 years old) at UCL under the ethical approval from the UCL Research Ethics Committee and informed consent obtained from all the participants (Deligianni et al., 2016; Deligianni et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the validation dataset sample.

claim: The data were obtained during rest, in which the participants were asked to open their eyes and remain awake with fixating a white cross on a black background.
source: The data were obtained during rest, in which the participants were asked to open their eyes and remain awake with fixating a white cross on a black background.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for data collection.

claim: The diagnosis of ASD was made based on structured interviews by a clinical expert for ASD in accordance with ADOS and DSM-IV-TR.
source: The diagnosis of ASD was made based on structured interviews by a clinical expert for ASD in accordance with ADOS and DSM-IV-TR (Lord et al., 1989).
evidence: This describes the diagnostic procedure for ASD participants.

claim: IQ was evaluated based on Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence.
source: IQ was evaluated based on Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence.
evidence: This describes the IQ assessment method.

claim: Handedness was scored based on Edinburgh Handedness Inventory.
source: Handedness was scored based on Edinburgh Handedness Inventory.
evidence: This describes the handedness assessment method.
